title: the serpent-arrows and Garuda
hook: why the snakes run from Garuda, and why Garuda would come to Rama

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda. A great wind, the snakes let go, a touch on the face. I'm your friend, don't ask why.

The arrows that were snakes didn't fight Garuda. The moment his wind reached the shore, they fled. People who grew up with Indian tales know why. They've heard it from grandparents, in comics, in temple carvings. It's a story about two sisters, a horse's tail, a cheat, and a son who will do anything to set his mother free. Valmiki doesn't stop to tell it, so here it is.
screen: `THE SNAKES DON'T FIGHT. THEY FLEE.` → `TWO SISTERS AND A HORSE'S TAIL.` → `A SON WHO FREES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: It's told in the Mahabharata's first book. Two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, are both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru is the mother of the serpents; Vinata is the mother of Garuda. The sisters bet on the color of a divine horse's tail, and the loser becomes the winner's servant. Kadru cheats: she has her serpent sons hang on the tail so it looks black. Vinata loses, and becomes a servant to her sister and the snakes. Her son Garuda asks the serpents what it will take to free his mother. Bring us the nectar of immortality, they say, from the gods. So Garuda storms heaven, wins the nectar, and frees her. On the way, Vishnu meets him and offers him a gift, and Garuda in turn agrees to serve Vishnu, as the bird he rides and the emblem on his banner. That's why snakes and Garuda are enemies, and why Garuda carries Vishnu. Now put that back on the battlefield at Lanka. The bird who carries Vishnu comes down to free Rama, calls himself his friend, and won't say why. For many Hindus that's a quiet sign of who Rama is: Vishnu come to earth. Valmiki doesn't spell it out here; he lets the reader notice. And so a week closes that ran from Vibhishana welcomed on the beach, to spies set free, a last offer at the gates, arrows from the sky, and a friend on the wind.
screen: `KADRU AND VINATA.` · `THE CHEAT ON THE HORSE'S TAIL.` · `GARUDA FREES HIS MOTHER.` · `THE BIRD WHO CARRIES VISHNU.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM REFUGE TO RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who, like Garuda, would cross anything for a person they love: a parent, a friend, a sibling, maybe you. Let their face rest in your mind for a few slow breaths, and simply be glad they're in the world.
Garuda, the great bird, old enemy of serpents since he freed his mother from Kadru's serpents. He carries Vishnu, and comes down to free Rama.
Your line: a friend on the wind. Next week, a giant wakes. Seven days of war, done.

howItsDone: Garuda's story from the Mahabharata's Adi Parva is often told to children, and in many Vishnu temples a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands.

options: storm heaven and bring the nectar.

original.note: Sanskrit amṛta: the nectar of immortality, literally 'not dying', from a-, not, and mṛta, dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: snakes and eagles just don't get along.
what it means: Garuda's enmity with the serpents goes back to his mother's servitude to Kadru and her sons.
what a scholar hears: the Garuda story is told in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, in the section often called the Astika Parva.

chat.says: What does an old story about two sisters have to do with Garuda saving Rama?
options: It explains why snakes flee him, and that he carries Vishnu, whom many see in Rama.
It shows Garuda was repaying an old debt he owed to Rama's father, the king.
It's where Garuda first learned the healing touch he later used on Rama's wounds.
chat.meaning: Kadru's cheat made snakes and Garuda enemies, and Garuda became Vishnu's carrier. For many Hindus, his rescue quietly hints that Rama is Vishnu.

Kadru.meaning: mother of the serpents, who cheats in the bet

Vinata.meaning: Garuda's mother, made a servant by the cheat

Kashyapa.meaning: the sage married to both sisters

Mahabharata.meaning: the great Indian epic where this story is told

Vishnu.meaning: the god Garuda carries; many Hindus see him in Rama

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva: Kadru and Vinata; Garuda wins the nectar and becomes Vishnu's carrier)

notes: The Kadru–Vinata story is summarized from the Mahabharata, Adi Parva (chapters around 14–30 in the vulgate); confirm the details used (the horse Uccaiḥśravas, the tail made to look black, the nectar as ransom).
Garuda becoming Vishnu's carrier and banner emblem in exchange for a boon: confirm.
The statement that many Hindus read Garuda's arrival as a sign of Rama's divinity is framed as a reading, not as Valmiki's explicit claim.
